sections.h: Ezekiel 8: four abominations in the Temple
sections.b: Ezekiel's vision of September 592 BC shows idolatry inside the LORD's own house: the image of jealousy at the north gate, engraved animals and filthy idols on a hidden wall before seventy elders, women weeping for Tammuz, and men bowing to the sun with their backs to the temple (8:3-16). Chapter 14 turns inward: elders sit before the prophet with idols "in their hearts" (14:3-7). Ezekiel keeps three words apart: gillulim "filthy idols", shiqqutsim "detestable things" and to'evot "abhorrent things".
sections.refs: Ezekiel 8:3-16; Ezekiel 14:3-7; Ezekiel 11:18; 2 Kings 21:1-9; 2 Kings 23:4-14; Jeremiah 44:15-19

sections.b: In Ezekiel the glory of the LORD leaves his house in stages: from the cherub to the threshold (9:3), to the east gate (10:18-19), and to the mountain east of the city (11:22-23). The people said the LORD had left the land (8:12); the vision shows that he sees all, and leaves because of what he sees. The glory returns by the same east gate in Ezekiel 43:1-5.
sections.refs: Ezekiel 9:3; Ezekiel 10:4; Ezekiel 10:18-19; Ezekiel 11:22-23; Ezekiel 43:1-5; 1 Kings 8:10-11; Exodus 40:34-35

sections.b: Ezekiel 10 says that the winged creatures he saw by the Kebar canal are cherubim (10:15, 20), the guardians of the Holy of Holies. The one change from chapter 1 is in 10:14, where the ox face is called the face of a cherub; the Talmud says Ezekiel's prayer made the change (Hagigah 13b), and Codex Vaticanus has no text at 10:14.

In Ezekiel 10:15 and 10:20 the prophet says that the "living creature" of chapter 1 is a group of cherubim. The wheels beside them are called by a second Hebrew word, galgal, "whirling wheel" (10:2, 6, 13), and the Plain keeps it apart from ofannim "wheels".

A man in linen is sent through Jerusalem to mark the foreheads of those who sigh and groan over the abhorrent things done in it; the six executioners are told not to touch anyone with the mark (9:4-6). The Hebrew word is the letter tav, written in the old script like a cross. Rashi says the sign protects the righteous; the Talmud has Gabriel write it in ink on the righteous and in blood on the wicked (Shabbat 55a); church fathers read it as the cross. Revelation 7:3 and 9:4 take up the picture.

sections.h: Survivors who tell, and survivors who comfort
sections.b: Ezekiel 9:8 and 11:13 end in the prophet's cry for the remnant of Israel. In 12:16 the LORD leaves a few alive to tell the nations of the people's abhorrent things; in 14:22-23 the survivors who reach the exiles prove by their conduct that the judgment was just, and so comfort them.

In 11:15-21 the LORD tells the exiles that, though the people of Jerusalem call them far from the LORD, he has become a "little sanctuary" for them where they are and will gather them and give them one heart. In chapter 12 Ezekiel acts out the exile by day and the leader's flight by night, with his face covered. Zedekiah was blinded and taken to Babylon (2 Kings 25:4-7).

sections.h: Prophets of peace, and the prophet who is deceived (Ezekiel 12-14)
sections.b: Ezekiel names marks of a false prophet: he speaks out of his own heart, says "the LORD declares" when the LORD has not sent him, promises peace where there is none, and does not repair the breaches (12:24; 13:1-16). He is paid in barley and bread (13:19). In 14:9 the LORD says that a prophet who is deceived has been deceived by the LORD, a hard line read as judgment on those who chose idols. Paul's "whitewashed wall" (Acts 23:3) draws on 13:10-15.
sections.refs: Ezekiel 12:24; Ezekiel 13:1-23; Ezekiel 14:9-10; Jeremiah 23:16-22; Jeremiah 28; Deuteronomy 18:20-22; Acts 23:3

sections.b: Ezekiel says that if a land sins and the LORD sends famine, wild animals, a sword or a plague, even Noah, Daniel and Job would save only themselves, not sons or daughters. The three are known for rescuing or praying for others (Genesis 7:1; Job 42:8-9; Daniel 2:24). The text speaks of a land whose guilt is complete; Ezekiel himself prays in 9:8 and 11:13.

Noah is named first of three men whose righteousness would save only their own lives (Ezekiel 14:14, 20). In Genesis 7:1 his household is saved with him; Ezekiel's point is that in a land under judgment even such a man could not rescue sons or daughters.

Job is the third of the three righteous men in Ezekiel 14:14, 20. His prayer for his friends (Job 42:8-9) makes him a model of intercession, which is the reason Ezekiel names him: even he would save only himself.

The Daniel of Ezekiel 14:14, 20 is written dn'l without the usual yod (the fuller spelling with yod stands at 28:3). Whether he is the exile of the book of Daniel or an ancient righteous king, Danel of the Ugaritic Tale of Aqhat, is debated; Jerome took him as the exile.

Israel is the LORD's vine in Isaiah 5 and Psalm 80. Ezekiel 15 asks what a vine is good for apart from fruit: its wood makes no tool, not even a peg, and burned at both ends it is fit only for the fire. The people of Jerusalem, who came out of the fire of 597 BC, are that wood. John 15:1-6 uses the picture of the branch that bears no fruit.

sections.h: Does the LORD deceive a prophet? (Ezekiel 14:9)
sections.b: Ezekiel 14:9 says that if a prophet is enticed, the LORD has enticed him. The same verb is used of the lying spirit in 1 Kings 22:20-23. Churches differ on how God's rule relates to sin and deception; see the cards on 14:9.

sections.h: One heart and a new spirit (Ezekiel 11:19-20)
sections.b: In Ezekiel 11:19-20 the LORD promises the exiles one heart and a new spirit, and to replace the heart of stone with a heart of flesh, so that they will keep his rules. The promise is repeated in 36:26-27, and 18:31 makes it a command.

sections.h: "My people, and I will be their God" (Ezekiel 11:20)
sections.b: Ezekiel 11:20 gives the covenant formula in a promise of return: after the new heart, they will follow the LORD's rules, "and they will be my people, and I will be their God." The same words close 14:11.

The Temple vision (592 BC) shows the sanctuary defiled by four abominations, then filled with corpses by the LORD's own command (9:7), and then abandoned by the glory. The LORD becomes a "little sanctuary" to the exiles (11:16), an idea some later readers took to mean the synagogue (Megillah 29a).

sections.h: The women with bands and veils (Ezekiel 13:17-23)
sections.b: Ezekiel 13:17-23 condemns women who sew bands on wrists and make veils to "hunt lives", for handfuls of barley and scraps of bread. The words are rare and the exact practice unknown; scholars compare Mesopotamian magic that used knots and cloth.
Ezekiel 13:5 says the prophets of Israel did not go up into the breaches or build a wall "to stand in the battle on the day of the LORD." Here the day is the Babylonian assault on Jerusalem.

In daylight Ezekiel packs baggage for exile, then at dusk digs through the wall and carries it out on his shoulder with his face covered (12:3-7). When the people ask what he is doing, the LORD says it is about the leader in Jerusalem and all the house of Israel (12:8-15). In 12:17-20 he eats his bread and drinks his water trembling, as a sign of the fear that will fall on those still in the land.

Ezekiel does not name Zedekiah, but the leader (nasi) who goes out through the wall in the dark, with his face covered, is taken as him. The LORD says he will be caught in a net, brought to Babylon, and not see it, and die there (12:12-13); 2 Kings 25:4-7 and Jeremiah 52:7-11 tell how he was captured, blinded and taken there.

sections.h: Ezekiel 12 on the people who stay
sections.b: Ezekiel tells the exiles that the sign of the baggage concerns the people still in Jerusalem: a few will survive the sword, famine and plague, and the cities will be laid waste (12:14-20). The warning comes in about 592 BC, almost six years before the city fell.

At the north gate of the Temple Ezekiel sees women weeping for Tammuz, another foreign cult in Judah. Jeremiah 44:17-19 shows women in the same years offering to the queen of heaven. Neither text links the two, but both show women's cult practice in Judah that the prophets condemn.

sections.h: Ezekiel counts the years from Jehoiachin's exile
sections.b: Ezekiel dates his visions by the years of King Jehoiachin's exile, which began in 597 BC (1:2; 8:1; 20:1; 24:1). The people left in Jerusalem said the exiles were far from the LORD (11:15); Ezekiel's vision shows the opposite, that the LORD is a little sanctuary to them (11:16).
